question: What is the typical age distribution of breast cancer diagnosis in Nigerian women compared to Western populations?

options.B: Diagnosed at a significantly younger age
options.C: Evenly distributed across all age brackets

explanation: Nigerian women often present with breast cancer in their thirties and forties, which is younger than the typical postmenopausal peak seen in Western countries. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h1)

question: Why is the mortality-to-incidence ratio for breast cancer generally higher in Nigeria than in high-income nations?

options.A: Higher biological aggressiveness of every tumor cell
options.B: Late presentation at advanced clinical stages
options.C: Strict government bans on standard chemotherapy
options.D: Complete absence of any surgical facilities

explanation: Most patients in Nigeria present at advanced stages III or IV due to delayed care-seeking, financial barriers, and reliance on traditional remedies, severely reducing survival rates. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h1)

question: Mutations in which specific genes are strongly linked to an inherited predisposition for breast cancer?
explanation: Inherited mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes significantly elevate the lifetime risk of developing both breast and ovarian cancers. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h2)

question: A patient asks why early menarche increases her chance of developing breast cancer. What is the physiological rationale?

options.A: It permanently alters the structural density of the skin
options.B: It blocks the normal lymphatic drainage of the axilla
options.C: It causes premature calcification of the milk ducts
options.D: It extends total lifetime exposure to estrogen stimulation

explanation: Early menarche means the breast tissue is exposed to proliferative estrogen signaling over a greater number of years before menopause. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h2)

question: What is the primary histological distinction between ductal carcinoma in situ and invasive ductal carcinoma?

options.A: In situ carcinoma has already spread to distant bones
options.B: In situ carcinoma only occurs in male breast tissue
options.C: Invasive carcinoma lacks any epithelial cell components
options.D: Invasive carcinoma has breached the basement membrane

explanation: Ductal carcinoma in situ remains confined within the milk ducts by the basement membrane, whereas invasive carcinoma breaks through this barrier to enter surrounding tissue. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h3)

question: What does the letter 'N' represent in the standard TNM cancer staging classification?
explanation: In the TNM system, N stands for nodes, indicating whether and to what extent cancer cells have migrated to nearby regional lymph nodes. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h3)

question: Which physical finding is classically described as 'peau d'orange' in advanced breast cancer?

options.A: Thickened, pitted skin resembling an orange peel
options.B: Deep ulceration directly over the nipple apex
options.C: Hard calcified nodules scattered across the chest wall
options.D: Bright yellow discoloration of the areola

explanation: Peau d'orange is caused by edema from dermal lymphatic blockage, creating a pitted skin texture that looks like an orange peel. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h4)

question: A patient presents to the clinic with a newly discovered breast lesion. Which characteristic is most consistent with a malignant tumor?

options.A: Soft, rubbery mass that slides easily upon palpation
options.B: Painful, tender swelling that fluctuates with menstruation
options.C: Symmetrical enlargement of both breasts simultaneously
options.D: Hard, irregular mass that is fixed to surrounding tissue

explanation: Malignant breast lumps are typically hard, irregular in shape, and fixed to underlying chest structures or skin, unlike benign fibroadenomas which are mobile. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h4)

question: What is the primary radiological screening tool used to detect non-palpable breast lesions and microcalcifications?
explanation: Mammography uses low-dose X-rays to image breast tissue, making it uniquely capable of identifying microcalcifications and small tumors before they become palpable. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h5)

question: Why is breast self-examination still encouraged in low-resource community settings despite limitations in advanced screening?

options.A: It prevents the initial genetic mutation from occurring in cells
options.B: It promotes general body awareness and prompts early reporting of changes
options.C: It completely replaces the need for biopsy and histopathology
options.D: It guarantees the accurate staging of internal lymph nodes

explanation: Regular self-examination helps individuals notice new lumps or skin changes promptly, encouraging earlier medical consultation rather than waiting for advanced symptoms. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h5)

question: Which surgical procedure involves the complete removal of the breast tissue along with axillary lymph node dissection?
explanation: A modified radical mastectomy removes the entire breast along with regional axillary lymph nodes while typically leaving the pectoral muscles intact. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h6)

question: A patient who underwent a modified radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection is at risk for lymphedema. What is an appropriate nursing intervention?

options.A: Instruct the patient to avoid blood pressure measurements on the affected arm
options.B: Apply tight elastic bandages continuously to restrict all arterial flow
options.C: Encourage heavy lifting with the ipsilateral arm to improve muscle tone
options.D: Administer prophylactic intravenous fluids through the surgical side

explanation: To prevent lymphedema, any trauma, venipuncture, or blood pressure cuffs on the affected arm must be strictly avoided to prevent impairing compromised lymphatic drainage. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of palliative care in patients with end-stage metastatic breast cancer?

options.A: Achieving complete permanent eradication of all cancer cells
options.B: Reversing previous surgical tissue removal through regeneration
options.C: Accelerating the natural metabolic decline of the body
options.D: Maximizing the quality of life and relieving distressing symptoms

explanation: Palliative care focuses on comfort, pain control, and psychological support when curative treatment is no longer effective or appropriate. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h7)

question: Why is psychological counseling considered a crucial component of breast cancer rehabilitation?

options.A: Counseling replaces the physiological need for analgesic medications
options.B: Patients frequently experience body image disturbance and emotional distress
options.C: Mental health support eliminates the risk of bone metastasis
options.D: Psychological therapy has been proven to shrink primary tumor size

explanation: Loss of a breast, hair loss from chemotherapy, and terminal diagnosis cause profound psychological trauma, making mental health support essential. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h7)

question: What is a major barrier that community health nurses frequently encounter during breast cancer awareness campaigns in Nigeria?

options.A: Cultural myths and reliance on traditional alternative remedies
options.B: Excessive availability of free screening mammograms
options.C: Lack of interest from patients due to total absence of disease
options.D: Mandatory government laws prohibiting surgical treatment

explanation: Misconceptions about the cause of cancer and reliance on traditional healers often delay timely presentation to formal healthcare facilities. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h8)

question: How do community health nurses best contribute to reducing breast cancer mortality in local populations?

options.A: By conducting educational outreaches that promote early detection and prompt reporting
options.B: By discouraging patients from ever visiting hospitals
options.C: By performing independent radical mastectomies in rural health posts
options.D: By manufacturing advanced chemotherapeutic agents locally

explanation: Nurses bridge the gap between community populations and healthcare systems by dispelling myths and encouraging timely medical evaluation for suspicious lumps. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h8)
